title: Thirteen
full_review:
A teen-age girl spirals down the self-destructive slippery slope of peer pressure in the unflinching cautionary drama "Thirteen" (Fox Searchlight).

First-time director Catherine Hardwicke, who co-wrote this study of adolescent turmoil with then-13-year-old Nikki Reed, takes an uncompromising, at times difficult-to-watch look at the hypersexualized, materialistic pressure cooker in which many young girls find themselves in pursuit of identity and peer approval.

At its dysfunctional core, the story hinges on the mother-daughter relationship between Tracy (Evan Rachel Wood), a clean-scrubbed seventh-grader who writes poetry and whose bed is still adorned with the teddy-bear-and-Barbie-doll props of childhood, and her divorced, single mother, Melanie (Holly Hunter), a hippie hairdresser with a past of substance abuse.

Tracy's unraveling begins when, after suffering the scorn of her junior high's catty fashion police, she ingratiates herself to Evie (Reed), a classmate who leapfrogged adolescent awkwardness in one summer, returning to school the object of every boy's lust and every girl's envy.

Commencing their friendship with a shoplifting spree, Tracy seals her initiation into the "cool" sisterhood by stealing a wealthy woman's wallet -- full of cash and credit cards -- and presenting it to Evie as a platinum tribute.

Tracy quickly graduates from theft to drugs to group sex. Under the guidance of her pubescent Pygmalion, Tracy revamps her wardrobe, replacing her Pollyanna threads with teen-slut-couture, complete with navel and tongue piercings.

Melanie, though devoted to Tracy, is utterly unequipped emotionally to deal with her daughter's rebellious transformation. But despite her maternal miscues, she comes across as a candidate for mother of the year compared to Evie's pill-popping, sometimes-model-mostly-barmaid stepmom (Deborah Kara Unger), who sheds more tears over her nip-and-tuck maintenance than her stepdaughter's out-of-control behavior.

Tracy's home situation -- a veritable commune for her mother's dysfunctional clientele -- is further complicated by the presence of Brady (Jeremy Sisto), Melanie's on-again, off-again live-in boyfriend and a recovering addict. Tracy resents Brady for taking the place of her father, himself an aloof workaholic, whose one token attempt at helping his daughter only exacerbates the problem. As the bleak story unfolds, it is revealed that much of Tracy's anger -- which at times manifests itself in self-mutilation -- is fueled by her parents' divorce.

While some may find its unfiltered depiction of adolescent angst and self-destructive behavior offensive, the film's strong performances, especially by the two teen leads, effectively capture the morally vacuous environment in which many young girls find themselves -- a hedonistic wasteland fueled by media-driven expectations of superficiality and a materialism gone wild. The extremes of past generations have become the norms of a contemporary teen culture. This generational myopia is visually distilled through a telling shot of Tracy standing near a billboard which reads "Beauty is Truth."

Another issue raised involves what psychologists refer to as "girl culture." Experts see early adolescence as a pivotal period in a girl's developing self-esteem and burgeoning sense of identity. It is often during this most vulnerable juncture when girls, denied the socially sanctioned forms of aggression afforded boys -- sports, roughhousing -- resort to equally violent, if less physical, alternatives such as fashion policing, forming cliques and cruel gossiping.

However, the film moves beyond psychological scapegoating, and stops the buck at the girls' respective parents and guardians, strongly suggesting that a stable home life is the best antidote for waywardness -- a point driven home by a darkly humorous scene involving one of Melanie's clients who tries some chicken-soup-for-the-soul-type, pop psychobabble on the feuding femmes.
Despite an ending that hints at redemption, the girls' real problem is that they are depending on adults who are just as immature, and, in many ways, less in control of their lives than themselves.

Due to several sexual encounters, recurring self-destructive violence and drug abuse, an instance of same-sex kissing, a scene involving full-frontal nudity, as well as much rough and explicit language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
